Time passed. Food went stale. Houseplants withered. Neighbors stared through the window at a frozen figure with a massive, unmoving smile... punctuated only by the minuscule movements of a hand on the mouse.

Trust me, they tried to close their MacBook. They really did. But every click meant more info, design galore, and... wait, more feet pics?

A year ago today, I was enjoying  break. A nice long break.

I dove down the rabbit hole and the more I read about their opensource culture, radical transparency, product, and voice, the clearer it became:

I didn’t just want to join. I needed to!

I reached out to James and Charles, and to make sure the team saw me, I applied as well.

Here’s to many more!

repost.content:
Rewriting local flag evaluation in Rust dropped our RAM usage from 270GB to 5GB.

The flags team moved PostHog's feature flag local evaluation endpoint from Django to Rust, and here's the before-and-after:

1. The endpoint is high-traffic by design. Server-side SDKs poll it every 30 seconds for flag definitions, reading cached data from Redis with no flag logic and no database on the hot path.
2. On Django, it ran about 30 pods, 60 CPU cores, and 270 GB of total memory
3. The Rust version handles the same traffic on 5 pods, 2.5 cores, and 4.8GB total. A 24x cut in CPU and 56x in memory.
4. Latency dropped too: p50 from 40ms to 4ms, p95 from 95ms to 20ms, p99 from 170ms to 37ms.
5. The dedicated node pool of memory-optimized instances is simply gone. So are the PGBouncer sidecars.

The endpoint did almost no compute to begin with, which is exactly why moving it next to the existing Rust flags service was overdue.

To read more, check out Patricio Tarantino's post on moving feature flag local evaluation from Django to Rust → https://lnkd.in/eTRqsVC2
